record_identity.title: Compromised Mistral SDK package executed credential-harvesting payload on import

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Mini Shai-Hulud / TanStack compromise affecting Mistral SDK releases
incident_identity.date_basis: Mistral states compromised npm packages were uploaded on 11 May 2026 and the compromised PyPI release on 12 May 2026; affected releases were removed within hours.

summary: Mistral reported that the Mini Shai-Hulud supply-chain attack on TanStack resulted in compromised Mistral npm and PyPI SDK versions being published. The compromised PyPI package `mistralai==2.4.6` executed malicious code on import, downloading a background payload that harvested credentials from common locations. Mistral reported no impact to its global infrastructure and removed the affected releases.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Mistral's security advisory identifies affected npm and PyPI versions, publication windows and indicators of compromise. It states that the compromised PyPI release executed a malicious script on Linux at import time and launched a detached process designed to harvest credentials.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The occurrence is a concrete AI-software supply-chain compromise in which trusted distribution channels carried malicious code into an AI SDK. The current VIGIL taxonomy does not cleanly represent package-signing/distribution provenance compromise as a selectable class without stretching existing provenance classes.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The occurrence expands VIGIL into AI developer infrastructure and demonstrates that governance of AI systems includes package provenance, third-party build dependencies, release integrity, credential exposure and response obligations.
assessment_boundaries: Mistral reports no impact to its global infrastructure.
The npm packages were compromised but Mistral reports their malicious code path was non-functional; the PyPI package did execute a credential-harvesting payload.
The public advisory does not quantify how many customers installed or executed the affected PyPI release or whether credentials were successfully exfiltrated from customer systems.

severity_assessment.materialised_consequence: A malicious Mistral PyPI release was publicly distributed and executed a credential-harvesting background payload when imported on Linux systems.
severity_assessment.affected_scope: Potentially affected developers and organisations that installed `mistralai==2.4.6`; the number of installations and confirmed compromised downstream systems is not public.
severity_assessment.seriousness_and_persistence: The malicious package could harvest credentials from developer systems and therefore created material realised execution risk, but public evidence does not establish the scale of successful downstream compromise or persistent customer harm.
severity_assessment.quantitative_information: Mistral identifies one compromised PyPI release and multiple npm SDK versions; the malicious PyPI package was available for approximately three hours before removal.
severity_assessment.evidentiary_limits: Mistral reports no impact to its global infrastructure. The npm packages were compromised but Mistral reports their malicious code path was non-functional; the PyPI package did execute a credential-harvesting payload. The public advisory does not quantify how many customers installed or executed the affected PyPI release or whether credentials were successfully exfiltrated from customer systems.
severity_assessment.band_rationale: S3 rather than S2 is appropriate because a malicious credential-harvesting payload was actually distributed and executable, but confirmed downstream compromise at substantial scale is not established. S3 rather than S4 is appropriate because this exceeded a minor defect: the distributed package executed attacker-controlled credential-harvesting code.
